newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Assembly votes to lift state ban on ferrets.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Assembly votes to lift state ban on ferrets.

text.p: California's Assembly voted Thursday to let people keep ferrets as pets despite warnings that the furry-faced animal could undermine native species in the state.
The state Assembly burst into cheers when the ferret bill, introduced by Republican Assemblyman Jan Goldsmith, was passed on a vote of 59-to-7. It now moves to the state Senate.

Ferret ownership is illegal in only two states in United States, California and Hawaii. Anyone caught in California with a ferret faces up to a $2,000 fine; the animals are confiscated and euthanized or ordered out of state.

Often described as a cross between a kitten and a two-year-old child, the cuddly and playful ferret, with its long body and pointy tail, is popular in many states as a house pet and prized in Europe and Canada as a hunter of rodents and rabbits.

Opponents of the bill argue that California's size and climate afford too many opportunities for non-native wildlife to proliferate and upset the natural food chain by competing with indigenous animal populations.
They also fear the introduction of new animal diseases.
"We ought to kill the bill and every little ferret we can get our hands on," said state Assemblyman Dick Floyd, a Democrat, during Thursday's ferret debate. "This is a dirty rotten bill."
Supporters of the bill say California's ferret ban violates private property rights. They also assert that ferrets make excellent pets and could not survive in the wild.
People are far more likely to get bitten by a dog than a ferret, Goldsmith said. "Nowhere in this country is there any real threat," he added.
The bill would allow the domestic ferret to be owned as a pet without a permit, but would require ferrets to be licensed like dogs. The bill would also require ferrets to be spayed or neutered.
